strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: automatically allocating rank and sparsity budgets across LLM layers without manual thresholds, avoiding heuristic singular-value cutoffs used in prior low-rank+sparse methods.

The two-stage design (RPCA decomposition to constrain the search space, followed by REINFORCE-based probabilistic pruning) is a reasonably elegant way to avoid expensive backpropagation-based fine-tuning while jointly optimizing rank and sparsity.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple model families and scales (LLaMA 7B/13B/30B, LLaMA-2, BERT-base, DeBERTaV3), multiple compression ratios, and multiple baselines (SparseGPT, WANDA, BESA, LoSparse, LPAF).

Useful ablations (effect of RPCA iterations, heuristic threshold-based pruning, per-layer rank distribution, sequential layer pruning analysis) that provide some insight into method behavior and the necessity of combining low-rank and sparse components.
Reports consistent, if modest, improvements over pruning-only baselines (SparseGPT, WANDA, BESA) in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy across model scales.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix F (Theorem F.1, Lemma F.2, Corollary F.3) is superficial: the 'proof' is a single vague paragraph invoking 'RPCA recovery bounds' and 'PAC-Bayes generalization' without any actual derivation, and constants/assumptions (e.g., incoherence conditions required for RPCA guarantees) are never specified or verified for LLM weight matrices, making these claims unsubstantiated.

The most directly comparable baselines (LoSparse, LPAF), which are also low-rank+sparse composite methods, are not evaluated on the main LLaMA models in the primary results table; instead they are relegated to the appendix and tested only on much smaller models (BERT-base/DeBERTaV3-base), weakening the central claim that the method 'significantly surpasses...composite approximation' methods.

Reported perplexity/accuracy gains over the strongest pruning baseline (BESA) are relatively modest (e.g., ~0.2-0.3 PPL, ~1 point zero-shot accuracy), with no variance/standard deviation reported despite the method's inherent stochasticity (Bernoulli sampling, policy gradient), making it hard to assess statistical significance.

Key technical components (RPCA via ADMM, REINFORCE policy gradients, moving-average baselines) are individually well-established; the novelty largely lies in their combination for LLM compression, which is somewhat incremental relative to prior low-rank+sparse and probabilistic pruning literature.

No quantitative wall-clock or memory comparisons are provided beyond qualitative statements ('a few minutes', 'comparable to WANDA'), limiting reproducibility of the claimed efficiency advantages, especially for larger 30B-scale models.

The manuscript has notable presentation/proofreading issues (duplicated/overlapping section 3 'Preliminary' and section 4 'Preliminaries' headers, typos such as 'lmpact Statement'), suggesting insufficient polish.

Ablation in Table 3 shows extreme instability (PPL exceeding 2900 or NaN) under simple threshold pruning, but the paper does not clarify whether the proposed probabilistic method is similarly sensitive to hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, number of policy-gradient iterations) or robust by design, leaving open questions about robustness/tuning sensitivity.

Some qualitative explanations (e.g., early-layer pruning improving performance, last-layer anomaly in Figure 3) are asserted without rigorous investigation or statistical support, weakening interpretive claims.

strengths: The core idea of using RPCA to automatically determine low-rank/sparse decomposition (avoiding manual singular-value thresholds) combined with a policy-gradient-based Bernoulli masking scheme for budget allocation across layers is a reasonable and relatively intuitive extension of prior low-rank+sparse compression work.

The empirical evaluation spans a reasonably wide set of models (LLaMA 7B/13B/30B, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, BERT-base, DeBERTaV3-base) and compares against several relevant baselines (SparseGPT, WANDA, BESA, LoSparse, LPAF).
Ablations on RPCA iteration count and on heuristic vs. probabilistic thresholding provide some insight into the behavior of the decomposition stage.
The paper includes reproducibility artifacts (code structure description, hyperparameters) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical contribution (Appendix F: Theorem F.1, Lemma F.2, Corollary F.3) is superficial and not rigorously proven; the 'proof' is a one-line hand-wave invoking generic RPCA recovery bounds and PAC-Bayes without connecting to the specific Bernoulli/policy-gradient masking mechanism, and constants C, D are left undefined and unconnected to the method. This reads as padding rather than genuine theoretical support.

The paper's central claim of achieving strong performance 'without large-scale fine-tuning or backpropagation' is undermined by its own Appendix B results, where CAP without fine-tuning (CAP1/CAP2) underperforms LoSparse, and only the fine-tuned variant (CAP4) is competitive — contradicting the main narrative built in the abstract/intro.

Reported performance gains over the strongest baseline (BESA) in the main table are often marginal (e.g., ~0.1–0.3 PPL, ~0.5–1 point zero-shot accuracy), with no variance/seed information, making it hard to assess statistical significance.

Claimed efficiency advantages (minimal memory/time overhead, 'a few minutes' for RPCA decomposition) are asserted narratively rather than substantiated with quantitative runtime/memory tables comparing against baselines at matched settings.

The manuscript has structural/editorial problems suggesting insufficient polish: duplicated 'Preliminary'/'Preliminaries' section headers (Sections 3 and 4), a typo in the Impact Statement header, and an Appendix A (Knowledge Neurons) that reads as generic filler only loosely tied to concrete experimental validation of the proposed method.

Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines two well-established techniques (RPCA from 2009, REINFORCE policy gradients from 1992) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the 'subspace orthogonality' property claimed for RPCA's L and S components is asserted without justification.

Table 2 shows extreme instability at low RPCA iteration counts (PPL exploding to 32497 at iteration 1), raising concerns about the robustness and sensitivity of the decomposition stage that are not thoroughly analyzed or discussed.

Comparisons in Table 8 mix fundamentally different compression paradigms (pretraining distillation, task-specific distillation, structured pruning, matrix factorization) without clearly establishing equivalence of parameter budgets or fairness of comparison conditions.

No comparison against more recent/stronger baselines (e.g., quantization-aware methods, LLM-Pruner, or other 2023–2024 structured pruning/composite approximation methods beyond those already covered), limiting confidence in the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: manual singular-value thresholds and independent optimization of low-rank/sparse components in prior 'low-rank + sparse' compression methods.

The two-stage design (RPCA decomposition to reduce search space, followed by Bernoulli/policy-gradient-based global pruning) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination that avoids heuristic thresholds and large-scale backpropagation.
Broad empirical evaluation across multiple model families and sizes (LLaMA 7B/13B/30B, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, BERT-base, DeBERTaV3-base) and multiple baselines (SparseGPT, WANDA, BESA, LoSparse, LPAF).

Reasonably thorough ablations (RPCA iteration count, heuristic-threshold vs. probabilistic pruning, rank distribution analysis, layer-wise perplexity change analysis) that give some insight into method behavior.
Consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over baselines at 50% and 75% compression ratios, and additional results under higher compression ratios in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix F (Theorem F.1, Lemma F.2, Corollary F.3) is superficial: constants C, D are undefined 'data-dependent constants,' the 'proof' is a single unsubstantiated sentence citing RPCA recovery bounds and PAC-Bayes generalization without derivation, and the bounds do not appear to be used anywhere in the main method or experiments. This reads as decorative rather than rigorous theory.

The comparison with the most directly relevant baseline (LoSparse, Appendix B) shows that CAP without fine-tuning (CAP1/CAP2, i.e., the core proposed contribution) underperforms LoSparse, and only CAP variants with full-parameter fine-tuning (CAP3/CAP4) surpass it. This weakens the claim that the core RPCA+policy-gradient contribution alone is superior, and creates some inconsistency with the main paper's claim of achieving strong results 'without large-scale fine-tuning.'

Improvements over the strongest unstructured-pruning baseline (BESA) in Table 1 are relatively small (e.g., ~0.2-0.3 PPL, ~1% zero-shot accuracy), and no variance/multiple-seed results or significance testing are reported.

Computational cost claims for RPCA decomposition (e.g., 'a few minutes' for all matrices in a 7B model over ten ADMM iterations) are asserted without a detailed wall-clock/complexity comparison against baselines, which is important given that ADMM with repeated SVDs on large matrices can be costly.

Presentation/editing issues suggest the paper was not carefully proofread: a duplicated 'Preliminary'/'Preliminaries' section (Sections 3 and 4), a typo in the Impact Statement heading ('lmpact Statement'), and the acronym 'CAP' is used throughout experiments/appendices but is never formally introduced in the main text.

Some qualitative findings (e.g., unexpected perplexity improvement when pruning the last layer, or when pruning the first layer) are reported but not adequately analyzed or explained, leaving interesting but under-investigated observations.

The method's policy-gradient optimization uses a very small number of iterations (3) and modest calibration set (128 sequences), raising questions about optimization stability/convergence that are not deeply analyzed beyond the RPCA-iteration ablation.
